entries.d181f63090b7d4a1c0d7870c13a29306fadf0837: <div sID="gen11849" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="76" osisID="Ps.76" sID="Ps.76"/> <div eID="gen11849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11850" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11851" type="x-p"/> This psalm seems to have been penned upon occasion of some great victory obtained by the church over some threatening enemy or other, and designed to grace the triumph. The LXX. calls it, "A song upon the Assyrians," whence many good interpreters conjecture that it was penned when Sennacherib's army, then besieging Jerusalem, was entirely cut off by a destroying angel in Hezekiah's time; and several passages in the psalm are very applicable to that work of wonder: but there was a religious triumph upon occasion of another victory, in Jehoshaphat's time, which might as well be the subject of this psalm (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.28">2 Chron. xx. 28</reference>), and it might be called "a song of Asaph" because always sung by the sons of Asaph. Or it might be penned by Asaph who lived in David's time, upon occasion of the many triumphs with which God delighted to honour that reign. Upon occasion of this glorious victory, whatever it was, I. The psalmist congratulates the happiness of the church in having God so nigh, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.1-Ps.76.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. He celebrates the glory of God's power, which this was an illustrious instance of, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.4-Ps.76.6">ver. 4-6</reference>. III. He infers hence what reason all have to fear before him, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.7-Ps.76.9">ver. 7-9</reference>. And, IV. What reason his people have to trust in him and to pay their vows to him, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.10-Ps.76.12">ver. 10-12</reference>. It is a psalm proper for a thanksgiving day, upon the account of public successes, and not improper at other times, because it is never out of season to glorify God for the great things he has done for his church formerly, especially for the victories of the Redeemer over the powers of darkness, which all those Old-Testament victories were types of, at least those that are celebrated in the psalms.
entries.31d1a3cebda2533fc41448a85573c92e36a717ba: <div eID="gen11851" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11850" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Triumph in God.</title> <div sID="gen11852" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> In Judah <hi type="italic">is</hi> God known: his name <hi type="italic">is</hi> great in Israel. <hi type="super">2</hi> In Salem also is his tabernacle, and his dwelling place in Zion. <hi type="super">3</hi> There brake he the arrows of the bow, the shield, and the sword, and the battle. Selah. <hi type="super">4</hi> Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> more glorious <hi type="italic">and</hi> excellent than the mountains of prey. <hi type="super">5</hi> The stouthearted are spoiled, they have slept their sleep: and none of the men of might have found their hands. <hi type="super">6</hi> At thy rebuke, O God of Jacob, both the chariot and horse are cast into a dead sleep. <div eID="gen11852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11853" type="x-p"/> The church is here triumphant even in the midst of its militant state. The psalmist, in the church's name, triumphs here in God, the centre of all our triumphs. <div eID="gen11853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11854" type="x-p"/> I. In the revelation God had made of himself to them, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.1">v. 1</reference>. It is the honour and privilege of Judah and Israel that among them <hi type="italic">God is known,</hi> and where he is known <hi type="italic">his name</hi> will be <hi type="italic">great.</hi> God is known as he is pleased to make himself known; and those are happy to whom he discovers himself—happy people that have their land filled with the knowledge of God, happy persons that have their hearts filled with that knowledge. In Judah God was known as he was not known in other nations, which made the favour the greater, inasmuch as it was distinguishing, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.19-Ps.147.20">Ps. cxlvii. 19, 20</reference>. <div eID="gen11854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11855" type="x-p"/> II. In the tokens of God's special presence with them in his ordinances, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.2">v. 2</reference>. In the whole land of Judah and Israel God was known and his name was great; but <hi type="italic">in Salem, in Zion,</hi> were <hi type="italic">his tabernacle</hi> and <hi type="italic">his dwelling-place.</hi> There he kept court; there he received the homage of his people by their sacrifices and entertained them by the feasts upon the sacrifices; thither they came to address themselves to him, and thence by his oracles he issued out his orders; there he recorded his name, and of that place he said, <hi type="italic">Here will I dwell, for I have desired it.</hi> It is the glory and happiness of a people to have God among them by his ordinances; but his dwelling-place is a tabernacle, a movable dwelling. <hi type="italic">Yet a little while is that light with us.</hi> <div eID="gen11855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11856" type="x-p"/> III. In the victories they had obtained over their enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">There broke he the arrows of the bow.</hi> Observe how threatening the danger was. Though Judah and Israel, Salem and Zion, were thus privileged, yet war is raised against them, and the weapons of war are furbished. <div eID="gen11856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11857" type="x-p"/> 1. Here are bow and arrows, shield and sword, and all for battle; but all are broken and rendered useless. And it was done there, (1.) In Judah and in Israel, in favour of that people near to God. While the weapons of war were used against other nations they answered their end, but, when turned against that holy nation, they were immediately broken. The Chaldee paraphrases it thus: When the house of Israel did his will he placed his majesty among them, and there he broke the arrows of the bow; while they kept closely to his service they were great and safe, and every thing went well with them. Or, (2.) In the tabernacle and dwelling-place in Zion, there he broke the arrows of the bow; it was done in the field of battle, and yet it is said to be done in the sanctuary, because done in answer to the prayers which God's people there made to him and in the performance of the promises which he there made to them, of both which see that instance, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.5">2 Chron. xx. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.14">14</reference>. Public successes are owing as much to what is done in the church as to what is done in the camp. Now, <div eID="gen11857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11858" type="x-p"/> 2. This victory redounded very much, (1.) To the immortal honour of Israel's God (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou art,</hi> and hast manifested thyself to be, <hi type="italic">more glorious and excellent than the mountains of prey.</hi> [1.] "Than the great and mighty ones of the earth in general, who are high, and think themselves firmly fixed like mountains, but are really mountains of prey, oppressive to all about them. It is their glory to destroy; it is thine to deliver." [2.] "Than our invaders in particular. When they besieged the cities of Judah, they cast up mounts against them, and raised batteries; but thou art more able to protect us than they are to annoy us." Wherein the enemies of the church deal proudly it will appear that God is above them. (2.) To the perpetual disgrace of the enemies of Israel, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.5-Ps.76.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. They were <hi type="italic">stouthearted,</hi> men of great courage and resolution, flushed with their former victories, enraged against Israel, confident of success; they were <hi type="italic">men of might,</hi> robust and fit for service; they had <hi type="italic">chariots and horses,</hi> which were then greatly valued and trusted to in war, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Ps. xx. 7</reference>. But all this force was of no avail when it was levelled against Jerusalem. [1.] <hi type="italic">The stouthearted have despoiled and disarmed themselves</hi> (so some read it); when God pleases he can make his enemies to weaken and destroy themselves. <hi type="italic">They have slept,</hi> not the sleep of the righteous, who sleep in Jesus, but <hi type="italic">their sleep,</hi> the sleep of sinners, that shall awake to everlasting shame and contempt. [2.] The men of might can no more <hi type="italic">find their hands</hi> than the stout-hearted can their spirit. As the bold men are cowed, so the strong men are lamed, and cannot so much as find their hands, to save their own heads, much less to hurt their enemies. [3.] The chariots and horses may be truly said to be <hi type="italic">cast into a dead sleep</hi> when their drivers and their riders were so. God did but speak the word, as the God of Jacob that commands deliverances for Jacob, and, at his rebuke, the chariot and horse were both cast into a dead sleep. When the men were laid dead upon the spot by the destroying angel the chariot and horse were not at all formidable. See the power and efficacy of God's rebukes. With what pleasure may we Christians apply all this to the advantages we enjoy by the Redeemer! It is through him that God is known; it is in him that God's name is great; to him it is owing that God has a tabernacle and a dwelling-place in his church. He it was that vanquished the strong man armed, spoiled principalities and powers, and made a show of them openly.
entries.30ef40e6475c71eaa70429602e8e93480a072b6c: <div eID="gen11858" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Defence and Glory of Israel.</title> <div sID="gen11859" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Thou, <hi type="italic">even</hi> thou, <hi type="italic">art</hi> to be feared: and who may stand in thy sight when once thou art angry? 8 Thou didst cause judgment to be heard from heaven; the earth feared, and was still, <hi type="super">9</hi> When God arose to judgment, to save all the meek of the earth. Selah. <hi type="super">10</hi> Surely the wrath of man shall praise thee: the remainder of wrath shalt thou restrain. <hi type="super">11</hi> Vow, and pay unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God: let all that be round about him bring presents unto him that ought to be feared. <hi type="super">12</hi> He shall cut off the spirit of princes: <hi type="italic">he is</hi> terrible to the kings of the earth. <div eID="gen11859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11860" type="x-p"/> This glorious victory with which God had graced and blessed his church is here made to speak three things:— <div eID="gen11860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11861" type="x-p"/> I. Terror to God's enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.7-Ps.76.9">v. 7-9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou, even thou, art to be feared;</hi> thy majesty is to be reverenced, thy sovereignty to be submitted to, and thy justice to be dreaded by those that have offended thee." Let all the world learn by this event to stand in awe of the great God. 1. Let all be afraid of his wrath against the daring impiety of sinners: <hi type="italic">Who may stand in thy sight from the minute that thou art angry?</hi> If God be a consuming fire, how can chaff and stubble stand before him, though his <hi type="italic">anger be kindled but a little?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.12">Ps. ii. 12</reference>. 2. Let all be afraid of his jealousy for oppressed innocency and the injured cause of his own people: "<hi type="italic">Thou didst cause judgment to be heard from heaven,</hi> then <hi type="italic">when thou didst arise to save all the meek of the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.8-Ps.76.9">v. 8, 9</reference>); and then <hi type="italic">the earth feared and was still,</hi> waiting what would be the issue of those glorious appearances of thine." Note, (1.) God's people are the <hi type="italic">meek of the earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.3">Zech. ii. 3</reference>), the <hi type="italic">quiet in the land</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.20">Ps. xxxv. 20</reference>), that can bear any wrong, but do none. (2.) Though the meek of the earth are by their meekness exposed to injury, yet God will, sooner or later, appear for their salvation, and plead their cause. (3.) When God comes to save <hi type="italic">all the meek of the earth,</hi> he will <hi type="italic">cause judgment to be heard from heaven;</hi> he will make the world know that he is angry at the oppressors of his people, and takes what is done against them as done against himself. The righteous God long seems to keep silence, yet, sooner or later, he will make judgment to be heard. (4.) When God is speaking judgment from heaven it is time for the earth to compose itself into an awful and reverent silence: <hi type="italic">The earth feared and was still,</hi> as silence is made by proclamation when the court sits. <hi type="italic">Be still and know that I am God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.46.10">Ps. xlvi. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">Be silent, O all flesh! before the Lord, for he is raised</hi> up to judgment, <reference osisRef="Zech.2.13">Zech. ii. 13</reference>. Those that suppose this psalm to have been penned upon the occasion of the routing of Sennacherib's army take it for granted that the descent of the destroying angel, who did the execution, was accompanied with thunder, by which <hi type="italic">God caused judgment to be heard from heaven,</hi> and that the earth feared (that is, there was an earthquake), but it was soon over. But this is altogether uncertain. <div eID="gen11861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11862" type="x-p"/> II. Comfort to God's people, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.10">v. 10</reference>. We live in a very angry provoking world; we often feel much, and are apt to fear more, from the wrath of man, which seems boundless. But this is a great comfort to us, 1. That as far as God permits the wrath of man to break forth at any time he will make it turn to his praise, will bring honour to himself and serve his own purposes by it: <hi type="italic">Surely the wrath of man shall praise thee,</hi> not only by the checks given to it, when it shall be forced to confess its own impotency, but even by the liberty given to it for a time. The hardships which God's people suffer by the wrath of their enemies are made to redound to the glory of God and his grace; and the more <hi type="italic">the heathen rage</hi> and plot <hi type="italic">against the Lord and his anointed</hi> the more will God be praised for setting <hi type="italic">his King upon his holy hill of Zion</hi> in spite of them, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1">Ps. ii. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">6</reference>. When the heavenly hosts make this the matter of their thanksgiving-song that God has <hi type="italic">taken to himself his great power and has reigned, though the nations were angry</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.17-Rev.11.18">Rev. xi. 17, 18</reference>), then the wrath of man adds lustre to the praises of God. 2. That what will not turn to his praise shall not be suffered to break out: <hi type="italic">The remainder of wrath shalt thou restrain.</hi> Men must never permit sin, because they cannot check it when they will; but God can. He can set bounds to the wrath of man, as he does to the raging sea. <hi type="italic">Hitherto it shall come and no further; here shall its proud waves be stayed.</hi> God restrained the remainder of Sennacherib's rage, for he put <hi type="italic">a hook in his nose and a bridle in his jaws</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.29">Isa. xxxvii. 29</reference>); and, though he permitted him to talk big, he restrained him from doing what he designed. <div eID="gen11862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11863" type="x-p"/> III. Duty to all, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.11-Ps.76.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. Let all submit themselves to this great God and become his loyal subjects. Observe, 1. The duty required of us all, all that are about him, that have any dependence upon him or any occasion to approach to him; and who is there that has not? We are therefore every one of us commanded to do our homage to the King of kings: <hi type="italic">Vow and pay;</hi> that is, take an oath of allegiance to him and make conscience of keeping it. Vow to be his, and pay what you vow. Bind your souls with a bond to him (for that is the nature of a vow), and then live up to the obligations you have laid upon yourselves; for <hi type="italic">better it is not to vow than to vow and not to pay.</hi> And, having taken him for our King, let us bring presents to him, as subjects to their sovereign, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.27">1 Sam. x. 27</reference>. <hi type="italic">Send you the lamb to the ruler of the land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.16.1">Isa. xvi. 1</reference>. Not that God needs any present we can bring, or can be benefited by it; but thus we must give him honour and own that we have our all from him. Our prayers and praises, and especially our hearts, are the presents we should bring to the Lord our God. 2. The reasons to enforce this duty: <hi type="italic">Render to all their due, fear to whom fear is due;</hi> and is it not due to God? Yes; (1.) He ought to be feared: <hi type="italic">He is the fear</hi> (so the word is); his name is glorious and fearful,; and he is the proper object of our fear; with him is terrible majesty. The God of Abraham is called <hi type="italic">the fear of Isaac</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.42">Gen. xxxi. 42</reference>), and we are commanded to <hi type="italic">make him our fear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.8.13">Isa. viii. 13</reference>. When we bring presents to him we must have an eye to him as greatly to be feared; for he is terrible in his holy places. (2.) He will be feared, even by those who think it their own sole prerogative to be feared (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.12">v. 12</reference>): He shall <hi type="italic">cut off the spirit of princes;</hi> he shall slip it off as easily as we slip off a flower from the stalk or a bunch of grapes from the vine; so the word signifies. He can dispirit those that are most daring and make them heartless; for he is, or will be, <hi type="italic">terrible to the kings of the earth;</hi> and sooner or later, if they be not so wise as to submit themselves to him, he will force them to call in vain to <hi type="italic">rocks and mountains to fall on them and hide them from his wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.6.16">Rev. vi. 16</reference>. Since there is no contending with God, it is as much our wisdom as it is our duty to submit to him.  <chapter eID="Ps.76"/> <div eID="gen11863" type="x-p"/>

entries.1be7f329ba3c1dd8d81b44d2eea6a77fa3e1ec29: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6351"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 76</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.76.1-Ps.76.12">Psa 76:1-12</reference>. On Neginoth--(See on <reference osisRef="Ps.4.1">Psa 4:1</reference>, title). This Psalm commemorates what the preceding anticipates: God's deliverance of His people by a signal interposition of power against their enemies. The occasion was probably the events narrated in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.35">2Ki 19:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.1-Isa.37.28">Is 37:1-28</reference>. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.46.1-Ps.46.11">Psa 46:1-11</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen9733" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6351"/>1-2. These well-known terms denote God's people and Church and His intimate and glorious relations to them. <div eID="gen9733" type="x-p"/>

entries.b183f5cdeaa79f5b4fcc7df337304a0032abe800: <div eID="gen21044" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21045" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21046" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21046" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21045" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21047" type="x-p"/> The true God known in Judah, Israel, Salem, and Zion, <reference osisRef="Psa.76.1">Psa 76:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.76.2">Psa 76:2</reference>. A description of his defeat of the enemies of his people, <reference osisRef="Psa.76.3-Psa.76.6">Psa 76:3-6</reference>. How God us to be worshipped, <reference osisRef="Psa.76.7-Psa.76.9">Psa 76:7-9</reference>. He should be considered as the chief Ruler: all the potentates of the earth are subject to him, <reference osisRef="Psa.76.10-Psa.76.12">Psa 76:10-12</reference>. <div eID="gen21047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21048" type="x-p"/> The title, "To the chief Musician on Neginoth, a Psalm or Song of Asaph." Sae the titles to <reference osisRef="Psa.4.1-Psa.4.8">Psa 4:1-8</reference> : and 6: The Vulgate, Septuagint, and others have, "A Psalm for the Assyrians;" and it is supposed to be a thanksgiving for the defeat of the Assyrians. The Syriac says it is a thanksgiving for the taking of Rabbah, belonging to the children of Ammon. It is considered by some of the best commentators to have been composed after the defeat of Sennacherib. That it was composed after the death of David, and after the two kingdoms of Israel and Judah were separated, is evident from the first verse. If Asaph was its author, it could not be the Asaph that flourished in the days of David but some other gifted and Divinely inspired man of the same name, by whom several others of the Psalms appear to have been composed during the captivity. <div eID="gen21048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21049" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21050" type="x-p"/> In Judah is God known - The true God revealed himself to the Jews. The Israelites, after the separation of the tribes, had the same knowledge, but they greatly corrupted the Divine worship; though still God was great, even in Israel.
entries.70a1a51c084b25991a1ff29b981d1daebfc539ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21051" type="x-p"/> In Salem also is his tabernacle - Salem was the ancient name of Zebus, afterward called Jerusalem. Here was the tabernacle set up; but afterwards, when the temple was built on Mount Zion, there was his habitation. The Psalm was evidently composed after the building of Solomon's temple.
entries.8c978c4cb58dfffdbabf8a6bcf880aba7922f152: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21052" type="x-p"/> There brake he the arrows of the bow - רשפי rishphey, the fiery arrows. Arrows, round the heads of which inflammable matter was rolled, and then ignited, were used by the ancients, and shot into towns to set them on fire; and were discharged among the towers and wooden works of besiegers. The Romans called them phalaricae; and we find them mentioned by Virgil, Aen. lib. ix., ver. 705: - <div eID="gen21052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21053" type="x-p"/> Sed magnum stridens contorta phalarica venit, <div eID="gen21053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21054" type="x-p"/> Fulminis acta modo. <div eID="gen21054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21055" type="x-p"/> On this passage Servius describes the phalarica as a dart or spear with a spherical leaden head to which fire was attached. Thrown by a strong hand, it killed those whom it hit, and set fire to buildings, etc. It was called phalarica from the towers called phalae from which it was generally projected. In allusion to these St. Paul speaks of the fiery darts of the devil, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.16">Eph 6:16</reference>, to the note on which the reader is requested to refer. <div eID="gen21055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21056" type="x-p"/> The shield and the sword - If this refers to the destruction of Sennacherib's army, it may be truly said that God rendered useless all their warlike instruments, his angel having destroyed 185,000 of them in one night.
entries.42312ab455c0c3175d77bb8de5413ba56c03cc38: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen21056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21057" type="x-p"/> Than the mountains of prey - This is an address to Mount Zion. Thou art more illustrious and excellent than all the mountains of prey, i.e., where wild beasts wander, and prey on those that are more helpless than themselves. Zion was the place where God dwelt; the other mountains were the abode of wild beasts.
entries.fc24bc68e49e0fadc8de281ec17a2302dbaa829e: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21058" type="x-p"/> The stout-hearted are spoiled - The boasting blasphemers, such as Rab-shakeh, and his master Sennacherib, the king of Assyria. <div eID="gen21058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21059" type="x-p"/> They have slept their sleep - They were asleep in their tent when the destroying angel, the suffocating wind, destroyed the whole; they over whom it passed never more awoke. <div eID="gen21059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21060" type="x-p"/> None of the men of might - Is not this a strong irony? Where are your mighty men? their boasted armor, etc.?
entries.6fb64f64cc61726ce24ae91c95fab4662bf16941: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen21060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21061" type="x-p"/> At thy rebuke - It was not by any human means that this immense army was overthrown; it was by the power of God alone. Not only infantry was destroyed, but the cavalry also. <div eID="gen21061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21062" type="x-p"/> The chariot and horse - That is, the chariot horses, as well as the men, were <div eID="gen21062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21063" type="x-p"/> Cast into a dead sleep - Were all suffocated in the same night. On the destruction of this mighty host, the reader is requested to refer to the notes on 2 Kings 19.
entries.ad65aaefe7d04e2fed3a90303c6bb4f8220799ff: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen21063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21064" type="x-p"/> Thou, even thou, art to be feared - The Hebrew is simple, but very emphatic: אתה נורא אתה attah nora attah, "Thou art terrible; thou art." The repetition of the pronoun deepens the sense. <div eID="gen21064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21065" type="x-p"/> When once thou art angry? - Literally, From the time thou art angry. In the moment thy wrath is kindled, in that moment judgment is executed. How awful is this consideration! If one hundred and eighty-five thousand men were in one moment destroyed by the wrath of God, canst thou, thou poor, miserable, feeble sinner, resist his will, and turn aside his thunder!
entries.c818caeebdda0ed6c752f1c859e40000a250b678: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen21065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21066" type="x-p"/> Thou didst cause judgment to be heard - When God declared by his prophet that the enemy should not prevail, but on the contrary be destroyed, the earth the land, and by metonymy the inhabitants of the land, were struck with astonishment and terror, so as not to be able to move. The great boaster Sennacherib, who carried terror, dismay and desolation every where, was now struck with dumb amazement; and the angel of the Almighty, in a moment, stopped the breath of those hosts in which he confided.
entries.dfa7b0f234df0658c7ad840000cec9c9de3675db: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen21066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21067" type="x-p"/> The meek of the earth - The humbled or oppressed people of the land. The poor Jews, now utterly helpless, and calling upon the Lord for succor.
entries.8f397ea0875e4dc2a38e2c395d69abc969249c54: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen21067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21068" type="x-p"/> Surely the wrath of man shall praise thee - The rage of Sennacherib shall only serve to manifest thy glory. The stronger he is, and the more he threatens, and the weaker thy people, the more shall thy majesty and mercy appear in his destruction and their support. <div eID="gen21068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21069" type="x-p"/> The remainder of wrath shalt thou restrain - The Hebrew gives rather a different sense: "Thou shalt gird thyself with the remainder of wrath." Even after thou hast sent this signal destruction upon Sennacherib and his army, thou wilt continue to pursue the remnant of the persecutors of thy people; their wrath shall be the cause of the excitement of thy justice to destroy them. As a man girds himself with his girdle, that he may the better perform his work, so thou wilt gird thyself with wrath, that thou mayest destroy thy enemies. A good maxim has been taken from this verse: "God often so counterworks the evil designs of men against his cause and followers, that it turns out to their advantage and his glory; nor does he permit them to go to the extent of what they have purposed, and of what they are able to perform. He suffers them to do some mischief, but not all they would or can do." But how different is the reading of the Vulgate! Quoniam cogitatio hominis confitebitur tibi: et reliquiae cogitationis diem festum agent tibi: "The thought of man shall praise thee; and the remains of thought shall celebrate a feast day to thee." The Septuagint and the Ethiopic have understood the text in the same way. Some translate thus: "Certainly, the ferocity of the man (Sennacherib) shall praise thee: and thou shalt gird thyself with the spoils of the furious." The spoils of this great army shall be a booty for thy people. Probably this is the true notion of the place. The old Psalter renders it thus: For thoght of man sal schrife (confess) to the, and levyngs (remains) of thoght a feste day till the sal wirk. The paraphrase is curious, of which this is the substance: "When man forsakes perfitly his synne, and sithen (afterwards) rightwisness werks; it is a feste day; whenne the conscience is clered, and makes feste with the swetnes of goddes lufe, restand fra besynes of any creatur in erth: Than is God at hame with his spouse dwelland."
entries.f087d9c5c2fdeaa53af03c02c4cb3cf8cfb201ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen21069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21070" type="x-p"/> Vow, and pay unto the Lord - Bind yourselves to him, and forget not your obligations. <div eID="gen21070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21071" type="x-p"/> Let all that be round about him - All the neighboring nations, who shall see God's judgments against his enemies, should <div eID="gen21071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21072" type="x-p"/> Bring presents unto him - Give him that homage which is due unto him. <div eID="gen21072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21073" type="x-p"/> That ought to be feared - למורא lammora, "to the terrible One;" lest they be consumed as the Assyrians have been.
entries.28ddb5859843b7cd921ef7e7e640df6b120e1506: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen21073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21074" type="x-p"/> He shall cut off the spirit of princes - Even in the midst of their conquests, he can fill them with terror and dismay, or cut them off in their career of victory. <div eID="gen21074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21075" type="x-p"/> He is terrible to the icings of the earth - "He is the only Ruler of princes;" to him they must account. And a terrible account most of them will have to give to the great God; especially those who, instigated by the desire of dominion, have, in the lust of conquest which it generates, laid countries waste by fire and sword, making widows and orphans without number, and extending the empire of desolation and death. <div eID="gen21075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21076" type="x-p"/> Thus all are under his dominion, and are accountable to him. Even those whom man cannot bring to justice, God will; and to judge them is one grand use of a final judgment day.  <chapter eID="Ps.76"/> <div eID="gen21076" type="x-p"/>

entries.f74f56423bc10b792a3c9dcd4d9b5a4a032bf123: <div eID="gen9767" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Praise of God after His Judgment Has Gone Forth</title> <div sID="gen9768" type="x-p"/> No Psalm has a greater right to follow <reference osisRef="Ps.75.1-Ps.75.10">Psa 75:1-10</reference> than this, which is inscribed <hi type="italic">To the Precentor, with accompaniment of stringed instruments</hi> (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.4.1">Psa 4:1</reference>), <hi type="italic">a Psalm by Asaph, a song</hi>. Similar expressions (<hi type="italic">God of Jacob</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.75.10">Psa 75:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.76.7">Psa 76:7</reference>; <hi type="italic">saints, wicked of the earth</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.75.9">Psa 75:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.76.10">Psa 76:10</reference>) and the same impress throughout speak in favour of unity of authorship. In other respects, too, they form a pair: <reference osisRef="Ps.75.1-Ps.75.10">Psa 75:1-10</reference> prepares the way for the divine deed of judgment as imminent, which <reference osisRef="Ps.76.1-Ps.76.12">Psa 76:1-12</reference> celebrates as having taken place. For it is hardly possible for there to be a Psalm the contents of which so exactly coincide with an historical situation of which more is known from other sources, as the contents of this Psalm confessedly (lxx πρὸς τὸν Ἀσσύριον) does with the overthrow of the army of Assyria before Jerusalem and its results. The Psalter contains very similar Psalms which refer to a similar event in the reign of Jehoshaphat, viz., to the defeat at that time of the allied neighbouring peoples by a mutual massacre, which was predicted by the Asaphite Jahaziel (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.46.1-Ps.46.11">Psa 46:1-11</reference> and Ps 83). Moreover in <reference osisRef="Ps.76.1-Ps.76.12">Psa 76:1-12</reference> the “mountains of prey,” understood of the mountains of Seir with their mounted robbers, would point to this incident. But just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.75.1-Ps.75.10">Psa 75:1-10</reference> the reference to the catastrophe of Assyria in the reign of Hezekiah was indicated by the absence of any mention of the north, so in <reference osisRef="Ps.76.1-Ps.76.12">Psa 76:1-12</reference> both the שׁמּה in <reference osisRef="Ps.76.4">Psa 76:4</reference> and the description of the catastrophe itself make this reference and no other natural. The points of contact with Isaiah, and in part with Hosea (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.76.4">Psa 76:4</reference> with Hos 2:20) and Nahum, are explicable from the fact that the lyric went hand in hand with the prophecy of that period, as Isaiah predicts for the time when Jahve shall discharge His fury over Assyria, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.29">Isa 30:29</reference>, <hi type="italic">“Your song shall re-echo as in the night, in which the feast is celebrated.”</hi> <div eID="gen9768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9769" type="x-p"/> The Psalm is hexastichic, and a model of symmetrical strophe-structure.
entries.59a26cd0b9cc37cbf85be7ed06b055af865dc326: <reference osisRef="Ps.76.1-Ps.76.3">Psa 76:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen9769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9770" type="x-p"/> In all Israel, and more especially in Judah, is Elohim known (here, according to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.76.2">Psa 76:2</reference></hi>, participle, whereas in <reference osisRef="Ps.9.17">Psa 9:17</reference> it is the finite verb), inasmuch as He has made Himself known (cf. דּעוּ, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.13">Isa 33:13</reference>). His Name is great in Israel, inasmuch as He has proved Himself to be a great One and is praised as a great One. In Judah more especially, for in Jerusalem, and that upon Zion, the citadel with the primeval gates (<reference osisRef="Ps.24.7">Psa 24:7</reference>), He has His dwelling-place upon earth within the borders of Israel. שׁלם is the ancient name of Jerusalem; for the Salem of Melchizedek is one and the same city with the Jerusalem of Adonizedek, Jos 10:1. In this primeval Salem God has סוּכּו, His tabernacle (= שׂכּו, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.6">Lam 2:6</reference>, = סכּתו, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Psa 27:5</reference>), there מעונתו, His dwelling-place, - a word elsewhere used of the lair of the lion (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.22">Psa 104:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.4">Amo 3:4</reference>); cf. on the choice of words, Isa 31:9. The future of the result ויהי is an expression of the fact which is evident from God’s being known in Judah and His Name great in Israel. <reference osisRef="Ps.76.4">Psa 76:4</reference> tells what it is by which He has made Himself known and glorified His Name. שׁמּה, thitherwards, in that same place (as in fact the accusative, in general, is used both in answer to the question where? and whither?), is only a fuller form for שׁם, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.22.18">Isa 22:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.9">Isa 65:9</reference>; 2Ki 23:8, and frequently; Arab. <hi type="italic">ta̱mma ( tu̱mma )</hi> and תּמּן (from תּמּה) confirm the accusative value of the <hi type="italic">ah</hi>. רשׁפי־קשׁת (with <hi type="italic">Phe raphatum</hi>, cf. on the other hand, Sol 8:6)<note placement="foot">The pointing is here just as inconsistent as in ילדוּת, and on the contrary מרדּוּת.)</note> are the arrows swift as lightning that go forth (<reference osisRef="Job.41.20-Job.41.28">Job 41:20-28</reference>) from the bow; side by side with these, two other weapons are also mentioned, and finally everything that pertains to war is gathered up in the word מלחמה (cf. Hos 2:18). God has broken in pieces the weapons of the worldly power directed against Judah, and therewith this power itself (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.25">Isa 14:25</reference>), and consequently (in accordance with the prediction Hos 1:7, and <reference osisRef="Isa.10.14">Isa 10, 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.1-Isa.14.29">Isa 17:1-14, 29</reference>, Isa 31:1-9, 33, 37, and more particularly <reference osisRef="Ps.31.8">Psa 31:8</reference>) has rescued His people by direct interposition, without their doing anything in the matter.
entries.9f6190e9a63af71a75c9b4006a6400c4d64136e2: <reference osisRef="Ps.76.4-Ps.76.6">Psa 76:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen9770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9771" type="x-p"/> The “mountains of prey,” for which the lxx has ὀρέων αἰωνίων (טרם?), is an emblematical appellation for the haughty possessors of power who also plunder every one that comes near them,<note placement="foot">One verse of a beautiful poem of the <hi type="italic">Muḥammel</hi> which <hi type="italic">Ibn Dûchı̂</hi>, the phylarch of the <hi type="italic">Beni Zumeir</hi>, an honoured poet of the steppe, dictated to Consul Wetzstein runs thus: The noble are like a very lofty hill-side upon which, when thou comest to it, thou findest an evening meal and protection (Arab. <hi type="italic">'l - ‛š' w - ḏry</hi>).</note> or the proud and despoiling worldly powers. Far aloft beyond these towers the glory of God. He is נאור, <hi type="italic">illustris</hi>, prop. illumined; said of God: light-encircled, fortified in light, in the sense of <reference osisRef="Dan.2.22">Dan 2:22</reference>; 1Ti 6:16. He is the אדּיר, to whom the Lebanon of the hostile army of the nations must succumb (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.34">Isa 10:34</reference>) According to Solinus (<hi type="italic">ed. Mommsen</hi>, p. 124) the Moors call Atlas <hi type="italic">Addirim</hi>. This succumbing is described in Psa 76:6. The strong of heart or stout-hearted, the lion-hearted, have been despoiled, disarmed, <hi type="italic">exuti</hi>; אשׁתּוללוּ<note placement="foot">With orthophonic <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi>, vid., Baer’s <hi type="italic">Metheg-Setzung</hi>, §45.</note> is an Aramaizing <hi type="italic">praet. Hithpo</hi>. (like אתחבּר, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.35">2Ch 20:35</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Dan.4.16">Dan 4:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.3">Isa 63:3</reference>) with a passive signification. From <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.76.6">Psa 76:6</reference></hi> we see that the beginning of the catastrophe is described, and therefore נמוּ (perhaps on that account accented on the <hi type="italic">ult</hi>.) is meant inchoatively: they have fallen into their sleep, viz., the eternal sleep (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.39">Jer 51:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.57">Jer 51:57</reference>), as Nahum says (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.18">Nah 3:18</reference>): <hi type="italic">thy shepherds sleep, O king of Assyria, thy valiant ones rest</hi>. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.76.6">Psa 76:6</reference></hi> we see them lying in the last throes of death, and making a last effort to spring up again. But they cannot find their hands, which they have lifted up threateningly against Jerusalem: these are lamed, motionless, rigid and dead; cf. the phrases in <reference osisRef="Josh.8.20">Jos 8:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.27">2Sa 7:27</reference>, and the Talmudic phrase, “he did not find his hands and feet in the school-house,” i.e., he was entirely disconcerted and stupefied.<note placement="foot">Dukes, <hi type="italic">Rabbinische Blumenlese</hi>, S. 191.</note> <div eID="gen9771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9772" type="x-p"/> This field of corpses is the effect of the omnipotent energy of the word of the God of Jacob; cf. וגער בּו, Isa 17:13. Before His threatening both war-chariot and horse (ו - ו) are sunk into motionlessness and unconsciousness - an allusion to Ex. 15, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.43.17">Isa 43:17</reference> : <hi type="italic">who bringeth out chariot and horse, army and heroes - together they faint away, they shall never rise; they have flickered out, like a wick they are extinguished.  </hi>
entries.d7cd1e6790c188d01552ad46750c696fff2f5106: <reference osisRef="Ps.76.7-Ps.76.9">Psa 76:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen9772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9773" type="x-p"/> Nahum also (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Psa 1:6</reference>) draws the same inference from the defeat of Sennacherib as the psalmist does in Psa 76:8. מאז אפּך (cf. Rth 2:7; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.18">Jer 44:18</reference>), from the decisive turning-point onwards, from the אז in <reference osisRef="Ps.2.5">Psa 2:5</reference>, when Thine anger breaks forth. God sent forth His judiciary word from heaven into the midst of the din of war of the hostile world: immediately (cf. on the sequence of the tenses <reference osisRef="Ps.48.6">Psa 48:6</reference>, and on <reference osisRef="Hab.3.10">Hab 3:10</reference>) it was silenced, the earth was seized with fear, and its tumult was obliged to cease, when, namely, God arose on behalf of His disquieted, suffering people, when He spoke as we read in <reference osisRef="Isa.33.10">Isa 33:10</reference>, and fulfilled the prayer offered in extreme need in Isa 33:2.
entries.c7e58ab8f62372393aa486b555d7ac511d00cd57: <reference osisRef="Ps.76.10-Ps.76.12">Psa 76:10-12</reference> <div eID="gen9773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9774" type="x-p"/> The fact that has just been experienced is substantiated in <reference osisRef="Ps.76.10">Psa 76:10</reference> from a universal truth, which has therein become outwardly manifest. The rage of men shall praise Thee, i.e., must ultimately redound to Thy glory, inasmuch as to Thee, namely (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.1">Psa 76:1</reference> as to syntax like <reference osisRef="Ps.73.3">Psa 73:3</reference>), there always remains a שׁארית, i.e., a still unexhausted remainder, and that not merely of חמה, but of חמת, with which Thou canst gird, i.e., arm, Thyself against such human rage, in order to quench it. שׁארית חמת is the infinite store of wrath still available to God after human rage has done its utmost. Or perhaps still better, and more fully answering to the notion of שׁארית: it is the store of the infinite fulness of wrath which still remains on the side of God after human rage (חמה) has spent itself, when God calmly, and laughing (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.4">Psa 2:4</reference>), allows the Titans to do as they please, and which is now being poured out. In connection with the interpretation: with the remainder of the fury (of hostile men) wilt Thou gird Thyself, i.e., it serves Thee only as an ornament (Hupfeld), the alternation of חמה and חמת is left unexplained, and תּחגּר is alienated from its martial sense (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.17">Isa 59:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.9">Isa 51:9</reference>, Wisd. 5:21 [20]), which is required by the context. Ewald, like the lxx, reads תּחגּך, ἑορτάσει σοι, in connection with which, apart from the high-sounding expression, שׁארית חמת (ἐγκατάλειμμα ἐνθυμίου) must denote the remainder of malignity that is suddenly converted into its opposite; and one does not see why what <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.76.11">Psa 76:11</reference></hi> says concerning rage is here limited to its remainder. Such an inexhaustiveness in the divine wrath-power has been shown in what has just recently been experienced. Thus, then, are those who belong to the people of God to vow and pay, i.e., (inasmuch as the preponderance falls upon the second imperative) to pay their vows; and all who are round about Him, i.e., all the peoples dwelling round about Him and His people (כּל־סביביו, the subject to what follows, in accordance with which it is also accented), are to bring offerings (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.30">Psa 68:30</reference>) to God, who is מורא, i.e., the sum of all that is awe-inspiring. Thus is He called in <reference osisRef="Isa.8.13">Isa 8:13</reference>; the summons accords with Isaiah’s prediction, according to which, in consequence of Jahve’s deed of judgment upon Assyria, Aethiopia presents himself to Him as an offering (<reference osisRef="Isa.18.1-Isa.18.7">Isa 18:1-7</reference>), and with the fulfilment in 2Ch 32:23. Just so does v. 13 <hi type="italic">a</hi> resemble the language of Isaiah; cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.25.1-Isa.25.12">Isa 25:1-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Isa 33:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.18.5">Isa 18:5</reference> : God treats the snorting of the princes, i.e., despots, as the vine-dresser does the wild shoots or branches of the vine-stock: He lops it, He cuts it off, so that it is altogether ineffectual. It is the figure that is sketched by <reference osisRef="Joel.3.13">Joe 3:13</reference>, then filled in by Isaiah, and embodied as a vision in <reference osisRef="Rev.14.17-Rev.14.20">Rev 14:17-20</reference>, which is here indicated. God puts an end to the defiant, arrogant bearing of the tyrants of the earth, and becomes at last the feared of all the kings of the earth - all kingdoms finally becomes God’s and His Christ's.  <chapter eID="Ps.76"/> <div eID="gen9774" type="x-p"/>

entries.6021d93fcc8fc553b13564f8b20110d9816bd5d7:
PSALM 76
There is here celebrated the grace and truth of God in having, according to his promise that he would be the protector of the city of Jerusalem, defended it by his wonderful power against enemies, who were renowned for their warlike valor, and well equipped with everything requisite for war.
“Et bien equippez de toutes choses requises a la guerre.” — Fr.
To the chief musician upon Neginoth. A Psalm of Asaph. A Song.
This psalm, it is probable, was composed after the death of David; and, accordingly, some think that what is here described is that deliverance of the Jews from the Ammonites which took place in the reign of king Jehoshaphat. But I am rather inclined to adopt a different opinion, and to refer the psalm to that deliverance which they obtained from the Assyrians, recorded in 2 Kings 19. The Assyrians, under the conduct of Sennacherib, not only invaded Judea, but also made a violent assault upon the city of Jerusalem, the capital of the kingdom. The result of this is well known. They were compelled to raise the siege by the miraculous interference of God, who in one night destroyed that army with dreadful slaughter by the hand of his angel, (2 Kings 19:35.)
The inscription prefixed to the psalm in the Septuagint expressly mentions this as the occasion of its composition, Ωδὴ πρὸς τὸν Ασσύριον; “An ode against the Assyrian.” If in this the version of the LXX. is correct, and if Asaph, to whom the psalm is ascribed, was the person of that name who lived in the time of David, one of his compositions must have been adopted as suitably descriptive of this remarkable deliverance. He may, however, have been a different person of the same name, and was probably one of his descendants, as has been before observed, (page 159,) who lived in the time of Hezekiah. Bishop Patrick and Calmet are of this last opinion. Those who adopt the former suppose that the original reference of the psalm was to the victory obtained by David over the Philistines in the valley of Rephaim.
Hence the prophet, not inappropriately, affirms that God broke the arrows, the swords, and the shields. The point, however, which is chiefly necessary to be known and attended to is, that the continual care of God in defending the Church, which he has chosen, is here celebrated to encourage the faithful without any doubt or hesitation to glory in his protection.
Psalm 76:1-6
1. God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel. 2. And his tabernacle was in Salem, and his dwelling-place in Zion. 3. There he broke the arrows of the bow, the shield, and the sword, and the battle. Selah. 4. Thou art more glorious and terrible than the mountains of prey. 5. The stout hearted were spoiled, they slept their sleep,
“N’ont peu trouver leurs mains.” — Fr. “Have not been able to find their hands.”
and all the men of might have not found their hands. 6. At thy rebuke, O God of Jacob! the chariot and the horse were cast into a deep sleep.
 
1. God is known in Judah. In the outset, we are taught that it was not by human means that the enemies of Israel were compelled to retire without accomplishing any thing, but by the ever-to-be-remembered aid of Jehovah. Whence came that knowledge of God and the greatness of his name which are spoken of, but because He stretched forth his hand in an extraordinary manner, to make it openly manifest that both the chosen people and the city were under his defense and protection? It is therefore asserted, that the glory of God was conspicuously displayed when the enemies of Israel were discomfited by such a miraculous interposition.

Poole.heading: PSAL. LXXVI. To the chief musician on Neginoth, a Psalm or Song Or, for Asaph. of Asaph Or, for Asaph. Either, it was Composed by the Prophet Asaph; or Composed by David, or some other Holy Prophet of God, and committed to Asaph, or to his Posterity; It being usual to put the Parents name for his Children, of which I have formerly given divers Instances. The special and immediate occasion of this Psalm was unquestionably, some eminent Deliverance vouchsafed by God, to his People of Israel, and especially to Ierusalem, which the Psalmist thought fit to celebrate: But which and when it was, is both needless to enquire, and hard to determine..
